newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Zimbabwe holds private mine policy.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW-Zimbabwe holds private mine policy.

text.p: As a boom in minerals resources exploration begins to hit its stride in Zimbabwe, a senior government offical said on Tuesday that the southern African nation would continue its policy of enabling foreign firms to hold 100 percent ownership of their projects.

Zimbabwe hopes to encourage foreign miners to include more local companies and workers in new projects ranging from nickel and platinum to diamonds, but will not force the issue by demanding equity stakes in projects inside the country, Zimbabwe Secretary of Mines David Murangari said in an interview.

Asked whether at some point the government would seek to make government stakes in new projects mandatory, he said: "I doubt it." He said he believed Zimbabwe was getting a fair shake from foreign mining companies, although the government would push for greater roles for local companies in the future.
Zimbabwe has grown to be Africa's fourth largest gold producing nation and was becoming more of a force in other precious commodities, such as diamonds and platinum, he said.

Two weeks a go, Zimbabwe's reserve bank changed its policy on gold, enabling gold miners to be paid in U.S. dollars rather than local currency, Murangari said. "This removed a layer of cost for the industry," Murangari said.
Murangari acknowledged that Zimbabwe's bureaucracy was at times frustating to foreign business.
But he dismissed as "overblown" recent concerns by some foreigners that the government was creating problems for companies applying for work visas for employees.
He said the Hartley platinum project, 67 percent owned by The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd and 33 percent Delta Gold NL, both of Australia, would "put Zimbabwe on the map."
Hartley is due to come on stream next year.
Murangari said Zimbabwe's mining sector had taken on new significance in recent years after particularly as the agricutural sector has suffered from severe drought conditions.
The mining sector contributes about eight percent to the country's gross domestic product and earns nearly 45 percent of total foreign exchange revenue, Murangari said.
Receipts from mineral exports earned about Z$6.8 billion in 1995, Murangari said.
Currently, about 87 percent of Zimbabwe's surface in under exploration for different mineral deposits, he added.
Explorers are mainly looking for diamonds, followed by gold, base metals and platinum group metals, he said.
Political and economic changes coupled with the introduction of new technology making aeromagnetic maps of the entire country available has been behind the boom in exploration, Murangari said.
